subject: physics
question_text: Obtain an expression for the work done by an ideal gas during an adiabatic change, and explain it.

verification.note: Sourced from the Sri Chaitanya IPE Study Material for Jr. Students 2026-27 edition, physics volume, Chapter 12 Short Answer Question 7 (printed p.128). Only the question was taken; the answer, its steps and its mark split are original work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. The four-way 1+1+1+1 mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Physics hand-checked: for an adiabatic process PV^γ = constant, integrating P dV from V₁ to V₂ gives W = (P₁V₁ − P₂V₂)/(γ − 1) = nR(T₁ − T₂)/(γ − 1), and with ΔQ = 0 the first law gives ΔU = −W, so an adiabatic expansion cools the gas and an adiabatic compression warms it.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

steps.label: Setting up
lines: In an adiabatic process the gas
exchanges no heat, so ΔQ = 0, and
steps.margin_note: First mark. State ΔQ = 0 and the adiabatic relation PV^γ = constant.
steps.why: The whole derivation is built on two facts: no heat crosses the boundary, and the gas follows PV^γ = constant throughout the change.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to state ΔQ = 0 first — without it the integral below has no adiabatic meaning.
Writing PV = constant, which is the isothermal relation, not the adiabatic one.

recall.must_convey: That ΔQ = 0 in an adiabatic process, and the gas obeys PV^γ = constant.
accept: P V to the gamma equals a constant
reject: W equals P one V one minus P two V two over gamma minus one

steps.memory_tip: Adiabatic means no heat crosses the boundary: ΔQ = 0 is the first line to write.

steps.label: Carrying out the integral
lines: The work done as the volume
changes from V₁ to V₂ is
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Substitute P = K/V^γ before integrating — do not integrate a constant P.
steps.why: P is not constant in an adiabatic change, so it must be written as a function of V before the integral can be done.
common_mistakes: Treating P as constant and writing W = PΔV — that formula is for an isobaric process only.
Confusing the integrand: it is V^(−γ), not V^γ; ∫V^(−γ)dV = V^(1−γ)/(1−γ), which becomes a logarithm only if γ = 1 — the isothermal case, not this one.

recall.must_convey: That the work is the integral of P dV, with P replaced by K over V to the gamma before integrating.
accept: W equals integral of P dV from V one to V two
P equals K over V to the gamma

steps.memory_tip: P is not constant here: replace it with K/V^γ first, then integrate.

steps.label: The expression
lines: Using K V^(1−γ) = P V, the limits
and with PV = nRT this is also
steps.margin_note: Third mark. Both forms of the expression, in P–V and in T.
steps.why: PV = nRT turns the pressure–volume form into a temperature form, which is the one usually quoted and used in numericals.
common_mistakes: Writing (P₂V₂ − P₁V₁) in the numerator — the sign is reversed from the correct expression.
Leaving γ − 1 as 1 − γ without also flipping the sign of the numerator.

recall.must_convey: That W equals P one V one minus P two V two, all over gamma minus one, equal to n R times T one minus T two over gamma minus one.
accept: P one V one minus P two V two over gamma minus one
n R T one minus T two over gamma minus one
heard_as: P one V one minus P two V two
n R T one minus T two

steps.memory_tip: W = (P₁V₁ − P₂V₂)/(γ − 1): the SUBSCRIPT-1 quantity comes first in the numerator.

steps.label: What it means
lines: In an adiabatic expansion the gas
does positive work, so ΔU is
negative and the gas cools. In an
steps.margin_note: Fourth mark. State ΔU = −W and its two consequences: expansion cools, compression warms.
steps.why: The work in an adiabatic process is not extra energy from outside — with no heat supplied, it can only come out of the gas's own internal energy.
common_mistakes: Saying the temperature stays the same in an adiabatic process — that is the isothermal process, not this one.
Concluding the gas cools without first writing ΔU = −W to justify it.

recall.must_convey: That delta U equals minus W, so an adiabatic expansion cools the gas and an adiabatic compression heats it.
reject: P one V one minus P two V two over gamma minus one

steps.memory_tip: ΔQ = 0 forces ΔU = −W: the work has nowhere to come from but the gas's own internal energy.

insider_note: The sign in W = (P₁V₁ − P₂V₂)/(γ − 1) is the detail most answers get backwards — the subscript-1 state stays first.
